video_title: What to Own if the Tech Boom Falters | Steven Feldman
gist: Steven Feldman sees early cracks in the AI capital structure: falling token prices, CoreWeave bonds near 70 cents, an Oracle force majeure on an $18B Blue Owl data center, and Nvidia acting as a quasi-bank. He recommends taking profits and rotating into scarce, unlevered real assets (gold, electrification, copper, uranium, farmland). He reads Berkshire's Greg Abel succession and $370B cash pile as positioning to be the lender of last resort.

themes.theme: Cracks in the AI capital structure

insights.claim: Steven Feldman sees falling token prices (adoption is good, but the price charged for it is declining) and cracks in AI's debt-funded capital structure as signs of trouble in the AI trade.
insights.speaker: Steven Feldman
insights.so_what: Monetization per unit of AI usage is falling just as debt loads rise.
insights.quote: the price that you can charge for that adoption is going down

insights.claim: Feldman says CoreWeave bonds have cracked to around 70 cents on the dollar, calling it the canary for malinvestment in a capital-intensive business, because bondholders have no upside and are pricing real risk of non-repayment.
insights.speaker: Steven Feldman
insights.so_what: Credit markets are flagging AI infrastructure risk before equities.
insights.quote: the bonds cracked, and they're trading like at 70 cents

insights.claim: Feldman describes an $18B data center project (Blue Owl $3B equity, lenders $15B) where an energy pipeline permit was delayed and Oracle sent a force majeure notice, saying there is a reason it won't pay rent but is not in default; he says this is rare on projects of that size.
insights.speaker: Steven Feldman
insights.so_what: Permitting and power delays can turn data center leases into credit events.
insights.quote: Oracle sent a force majeure note

insights.claim: Feldman cites the CEO of Aon, one of the largest insurance brokers, saying potential losses are enormous and bigger than people are underwriting, and draws a cautious parallel to AIG's role in the financial crisis.
insights.speaker: Steven Feldman
insights.so_what: Insurers, the entities that price risk for a living, are signaling AI-linked exposure is underpriced.
insights.quote: The potential losses here are enormous. Bigger than people are underwriting.

insights.claim: Feldman argues Nvidia has become the bank, joint venture partner, investor and customer for a group of highly levered companies, making it as systemically important to the economy as JPMorgan.
insights.speaker: Steven Feldman
insights.so_what: Circular Nvidia financing concentrates systemic risk in one name.
insights.quote: They're probably now as important to the economy as JP Morgan would be.

insights.claim: Feldman advocates rotating out of AI winners and taking profits, noting holders of Hewlett-Packard and Dell are up 2-4x and argues they won't go up another 4x from here.
insights.speaker: Steven Feldman
insights.so_what: Take profits in AI hardware winners and reallocate.
insights.quote: It's okay to sell those.

insights.claim: Feldman argues AI-linked commodities and power don't need AI to be profitable: data centers that underearn still need electricity, the US had a transmission deficit before AI, and copper demand came from EVs and electrification first; momentum premiums in utilities will fade when 'the bloom comes off the AI rose', which he calls a when, not an if.
insights.speaker: Steven Feldman
insights.so_what: Hold the scarce inputs to electrification, but trim momentum-inflated utility names.
insights.quote: it's a when, it's not an if

insights.claim: Feldman's framework for inflationary environments: own scarce assets but not levered ones, because higher replacement cost lifts the value of scarce assets while rising rates can shrink the levered equity.
insights.speaker: Steven Feldman
insights.so_what: The test for any real-asset investment is scarcity combined with low leverage.
insights.quote: you want to own a scarce asset, but you don't want to own a leveraged one

insights.claim: Feldman notes that until about last year gold far outperformed gold miners because miners are capital-intensive and must keep tapping markets as rates rise, while the commodity carries no leverage.
insights.speaker: Steven Feldman
insights.so_what: Prefer the commodity, or unlevered operators, over capital-hungry producers.

insights.claim: Feldman says farmland has had only four down years in 50 (down about 3%) and is uncorrelated; his unlevered row-crop manager Goldcrest treats it as a 'get-rich-slow' scarcity asset, though farmer P&Ls are mixed with higher diesel costs offset by strong grain prices, and levered farmland equity is hurt by rates rising from 3% to 7%.
insights.speaker: Steven Feldman
insights.so_what: Unlevered farmland is a long-duration diversifier, but a hold over the next year.
insights.quote: it's had four down years in 50

insights.claim: Feldman's two most 'inevitable' trades are a monetary trade (gold, for sovereign debt pressure and geopolitical risk; flat for six months in a tight range despite higher rates) and an electrification trade (electricity, copper, uranium, pipelines, battery minerals, plus cyber protection).
insights.speaker: Steven Feldman
insights.so_what: His core portfolio tilt is gold plus electrification and supply-chain minerals.
insights.quote: if I could make two trades, I'd make electricity trade and a monetary trade

insights.claim: Feldman frames gold as an insurance policy, like term life: no one should own 100%, and if it doesn't work, everything else went up.
insights.speaker: Steven Feldman
insights.so_what: Size gold as a hedge, not a concentrated bet.

insights.claim: Feldman says the need for a US mineral supply chain independent of China is very important.
insights.speaker: Steven Feldman
insights.so_what: Domestic critical-mineral supply is a policy-supported investment theme.
insights.quote: we can't rely on China for these things

themes.theme: Berkshire as the lender of last resort

insights.claim: Feldman reads Greg Abel's selection as Buffett's successor as a signal: Berkshire will grind it out in real assets (railroads, pipelines, power) while sitting on $370B of cash waiting for something to break.
insights.speaker: Steven Feldman
insights.so_what: Berkshire's leadership choice signals real assets and patience over tech.
insights.quote: Sitting on $370 billion of cash, waiting for the thing to break.

insights.claim: Feldman predicts Berkshire may become the rescuer of last resort with a deal of around $50B, possibly saving a company like Oracle, because private-capital rivals like Apollo and Blackstone are themselves invested in the AI trade and will be licking their wounds.
insights.speaker: Steven Feldman
insights.so_what: In an AI bust, there may be few unencumbered sources of rescue capital.
insights.quote: I honestly think this will be 50 billion.

insights.claim: Feldman expects inflation to eventually come down as wars end and energy eases, China exports deflation from its manufacturing glut, and the AI trade dampens, and expects the US government to report inflation as low as it possibly can.
insights.speaker: Steven Feldman
insights.so_what: A disinflation surprise is possible even after hot prints.
insights.quote: I think inflation's going to come down.

insights.claim: Feldman argues the way out of the US debt problem is negative real rates, which requires understating ('fudging') reported inflation, while lived costs like tuition and medical care have risen about 10% a year.
insights.speaker: Steven Feldman
insights.so_what: Official CPI may understate real cost increases, eroding real returns.
insights.quote: you're going to have to fudge inflation

insights.claim: Feldman cites diesel at $8.85 a gallon at his local station and $100+ steaks in New York, attributing agricultural inflation to diesel and fertilizer (urea) costs from the Ukraine and Iran wars.
insights.speaker: Steven Feldman
insights.so_what: Energy-driven input costs are feeding through food supply chains.

insights.claim: Feldman says the luxury sector, including LVMH, has rolled over as aspirational buyers balk at prices like $9,000 Chanel skirts and $2,000-a-night hotel rooms, and warns that a falling 401(k) wealth effect will push companies to cut prices.
insights.speaker: Steven Feldman
insights.so_what: Spending driven by the wealth effect is fragile if equities fall.
insights.quote: the luxury sector has rolled

insights.claim: Feldman, agreeing with Lyn Alden's fiscal dominance view, says $2T deficits on $40T of debt are politically locked in, interest costs already exceed defense spending and are creeping toward Social Security, and long-end yields are a fiscal phenomenon worsened by AI debt issuance competing for capital.
insights.speaker: Steven Feldman
insights.so_what: Fiscal pressure is likely to keep long-end yields elevated regardless of Fed moves.
insights.quote: the long end is a fiscal phenomenon

insights.claim: Feldman is skeptical AI can grow the US out of its debt, arguing that consumers are maxed out and AI can only reallocate GDP, not create it, unless the US takes productivity from the rest of the world, which would be geopolitically destabilizing.
insights.speaker: Steven Feldman
insights.so_what: Don't count on AI-driven GDP growth to fix fiscal math.
insights.quote: You can't create GDP out of AI. You could just reallocate it.

themes.theme: Portfolio construction: diversify, don't buy the dip

insights.claim: Feldman argues buying the dip is a fallacy unless it is a true baby-with-the-bathwater sell-off of great franchises; cheap old-economy stocks at 3x cash flow become 10x if cash flow doesn't return.
insights.speaker: Steven Feldman
insights.so_what: Be selective after drawdowns instead of averaging down reflexively.
insights.quote: Buying the dip is not the strategy. Finding the winners and diversifying is the strategy.

insights.claim: Feldman cites a study that 90% of 100-year stock market returns came from fewer than 100 companies (about 77), and argues the S&P 500 works like a tax-free, low-fee (about 3bp at Vanguard) hedge fund that systematically drops losers and lets winners run.
insights.speaker: Steven Feldman
insights.so_what: Index exposure captures the rare big winners that stock pickers usually miss.
insights.quote: the S&P 500 or the Dow is like a hedge fund without taxes

insights.claim: After a decade saying 60/40 should be 100/0, Feldman is coming back to bonds: 10-year yields around 5% in a tax-deferred IRA and about 4% on cash are now reasonable, with 5-10% in cash as dry powder and the rest in assets uncorrelated to the S&P 500.
insights.speaker: Steven Feldman
insights.so_what: Fixed income is useful again as ballast and dry powder.
insights.quote: I'm beginning to actually even come back to the bond.
